text: Baby turtles head for the brightest direction. On a natural beach at night, that is almost always the sea, because the open water reflects moonlight and starlight, while the land behind is dark with dunes and trees.
That is why street lights and buildings can confuse them. Hatchlings may crawl towards a lit road instead of the water. So some beaches switch off or dim their lights in nesting season.

Once in the water, the babies swim against the waves to reach the open sea. After that, scientists think, they steer by Earth's magnetism, and remember the magnetic "signature" of their home beach for years.

frames.cap: Each winter, lakhs of Olive Ridley turtles crawl onto beaches in Odisha, all at once, to lay eggs. It's called an arribada.
The eggs stay buried in warm sand for about 45 to 60 days. Warmer sand makes more females!
The babies dig out at night and crawl towards the brightest horizon, usually moonlight on the sea.
They may sense Earth's magnetism. Years later, females return to the same coast to lay their own eggs.

sec.t:
Each winter, on a few beaches in [[@odisha|Odisha]], something astonishing happens. Over a few nights, huge numbers of olive ridley turtles crawl ashore together to dig nests and lay eggs. In good years, lakhs of turtles arrive at Rushikulya and Gahirmatha. This mass nesting is called an *arribada*, Spanish for "arrival".

Each mother digs a hole with her back flippers, lays about 100 eggs the size of ping-pong balls, covers them with sand and returns to the sea. She never sees her babies. About 45 to 60 days later, the hatchlings dig their way out together, usually at night when the sand is cool and fewer hunters are about.

The race to the water is short but deadly. Crabs, birds, dogs and jackals wait on the beach, and fish wait in the shallows. Of every thousand hatchlings, perhaps only one survives to grow up.

The survivors vanish into the open ocean for years. Scientists call this time the "lost years", because the babies are so hard to follow. Many seem to drift with rafts of floating seaweed, where they find food and shelter.

In [[@chennai|Chennai]], [[@volunteering|volunteers]] have walked the beaches at night every nesting season since 1988, moving eggs from busy beaches to safe hatcheries. Thousands of students have joined in.

sec.h: Ancient travellers in a modern sea
sec.t:
Sea turtles have swum the oceans since the age of the dinosaurs, alongside the [[@ocean-reptiles|sea reptiles]] of that time. Today, all seven kinds face trouble. Some drown in fishing nets, so many trawlers now fit trapdoors that let turtles escape. Others swallow [[@ocean-plastic|plastic bags]], which look a lot like [[@jellyfish-sting|jellyfish]], a favourite food of some kinds, such as leatherbacks.

Warmer sand is a new worry, since it produces more females. Lights are another. Along the coast of Florida, many towns now use dim [[amber|amber]] lamps near nesting beaches, a colour hatchlings notice less. On the darkest nights, around the new moon in the [[@moon-phases|Moon's cycle]], the glow from a single hotel can pull a whole nest of babies the wrong way. Turning it off costs very little and gives them a clear run to the sea.

text: Crocodiles and alligators are cousins, both members of a group called crocodilians. The quickest way to tell them apart is the snout and the teeth.

An alligator has a wide, rounded snout shaped like a U. When it shuts its mouth, the upper jaw covers the lower teeth, so you mostly see a row of top teeth. A crocodile's snout is narrower and more pointed, like a V. Its upper and lower jaws are about the same width, so teeth from both stick out when its mouth is closed. The giveaway is a big fourth tooth on each side of the lower jaw, which sits in a notch and pokes up like a fang.

st.prompt: Which group of living animals is most closely related to crocodiles and alligators?
st.reveal: Crocodilians and birds are the only living members of a group called archosaurs, which also included the dinosaurs. A lizard looks more like a crocodile, but it sits on a different branch of the family tree.

sec.t:
Colour helps a little. Alligators are usually dark, almost black. Crocodiles tend to be lighter, olive or tan.

Look closely at the skin. Crocodiles have tiny dark dots on almost every scale. These are pressure [[sensor|sensors]] that feel ripples in the water. Alligators have them only around the jaws. Those jaw sensors are very sharp. In experiments, alligators in a dark tank turned towards a single drop of water landing near their heads.

Crocodiles also handle salt water better. [[gland|Glands]] on their tongues push out extra salt, so many crocodiles live in [[@mangroves|mangroves]] and river mouths. Alligators have much weaker salt glands and stay mostly in fresh water.

India has no alligators at all, but it has three crocodilians. The mugger, or marsh crocodile, lives in rivers, lakes and even [[reservoir|reservoirs]] across most of the country. It has the broadest snout of any crocodile, so it is often mistaken for an alligator. In winter, muggers dig burrows in riverbanks and lie up in them on cold days.

The saltwater crocodile is the largest living [[reptile|reptile]]. Big males can grow longer than 6 m, about the length of a small truck. In India it lives in the Sundarbans, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Bhitarkanika in [[@odisha|Odisha]], where the 2025 count found 1,826 of them.

The third is the gharial, with a thin snout like a long pair of tongs. It catches fish with a quick sideways snap. Strictly speaking it isn't a true crocodile but belongs to its own family. It is critically [[endangered|endangered]], and most survive in the Chambal River.

People sometimes call crocodilians living [[fossil|fossils]], and their ancestors did live alongside the dinosaurs. Yet their closest living relatives are [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds]]. Like birds, crocodilians build nests, and the mothers of many [[species|species]] guard them.

A mugger mother will gently carry her hatchlings to water inside her mouth. Those same jaws that can crush a turtle can hold a baby crocodile without a scratch.

Crocodilians were hunted heavily for their skins in the twentieth century, and many kinds became rare. In the 1970s India started breeding muggers, gharials and salties and releasing them into protected rivers and wetlands. The American alligator made a similar comeback after hunting was controlled. It was once endangered, and now there are more than a million in Florida alone.

text: When glue is runny, it can flow into every tiny bump and crack on a surface. Even [[@paper-made|paper]] or wood that feels smooth is full of microscopic hills and valleys. The glue seeps into them and gets very close to the surface itself. Up close, its [[molecule|molecules]] are attracted to the molecules of the surface, a pull called adhesion.

Then the glue changes from liquid to solid. Some glues dry as water or another liquid escapes. Others harden through a chemical reaction. As they set, the glue's own molecules grip each other tightly, a pull called cohesion. Now you have a solid bridge, gripping one surface on one side and the other surface on the other.
A good glue needs both kinds of grip. If either one fails, the join comes apart.

sec.t:
People have been making glue since long before history was written. In Italy, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] have found [[@stone-tools|stone tools]] with traces of birch tar on them, left by [[@neanderthals|Neanderthals]] more than 100,000 years ago. Birch tar is made by heating birch bark without much air, until a sticky black goo oozes out. It was used to fix stone blades onto wooden handles.

Later peoples boiled animal skins and bones to make glue, and the ancient Egyptians used it on furniture. In India, craftspeople have long used natural resins from trees, and in many homes a paste of cooked rice or flour still sticks paper together. [[@stone-age|Stone Age]] toolmakers were, in a sense, the first chemists.

In 1942, the American chemist Harry Coover was trying to make clear plastic for gun sights. One of his chemicals stuck to everything and was set aside as useless. Years later, in 1951, Coover and a colleague came across it again and saw what it could be. It went on sale in 1958 as superglue.

[[@accident-post-it|Sticky notes]] started with a failure too. In 1968, Spencer Silver at the American company 3M made a glue that was too weak. It stuck, but peeled off easily. Years later, his colleague Art Fry used it on bookmarks for his church songbook, so they wouldn't fall out. The little yellow notes went on sale in 1980.

Living things make glue too. Mussels in [[@tide-pools|tide pools]] spin threads tipped with a [[protein|protein]] glue that holds firm underwater, something most human glues can't do. Scientists are copying it to make glues for surgery.

Spiders coat parts of their webs with sticky droplets to trap insects. Some caddisfly [[larva|larvae]] glue tiny stones into tube-shaped homes. And [[@power-gecko-feet|geckos]] climb walls without any glue at all, using millions of tiny hairs on their toes that are attracted to the surface, the same pull that helps glue hold on.

text: छऊ पूर्वी भारत का एक नाटकीय नृत्य है, जिसमें कहानी कहने के साथ युद्ध के दाँव-पेंच घुले हैं। नर्तक उछलते हैं, घूमते हैं, झुकते हैं और ऐसे वार करते हैं मानो किसी लड़ाई में हों। बहुत-से नर्तक रँगे हुए मुखौटे पहनते हैं, और संगीत ऊँचा और रोमांच भरा होता है, जिसकी अगुवाई गूँजते नगाड़े और एक तीखी आवाज़ वाला फूँककर बजने वाला बाजा करते हैं।

इसकी तीन मुख्य शैलियाँ हैं, जिनके नाम उनकी जगहों पर हैं: पश्चिम बंगाल का पुरुलिया, झारखंड का सरायकेला और ओडिशा का मयूरभंज। ये [[@ramayana|रामायण]], महाभारत, पुरानी [[mythology|पौराणिक]] कथाओं और स्थानीय किंवदंतियों की कहानियाँ सुनाते हैं।

sec.h: युद्ध के मैदान से आई हरकतें
sec.t:
छऊ की हरकतें नकली लड़ाई से निकलीं। नर्तक तलवार-ढाल या लाठियों से अभ्यास करते हैं और योद्धाओं की तरह लात चलाना, कूदना और घूमना सीखते हैं। बहुत-से जानकार मानते हैं कि यह नाच उन कसरतों से पनपा, जिनसे कभी सिपाही और गाँव वाले खुद को चुस्त रखते थे।

इससे छऊ उन भारतीय परंपराओं से जुड़ता है जहाँ लड़ाई और नाच मिलते हैं, जैसे केरल का [[@sport-kalaripayattu|कलरिपयट्टु]]। छऊ में कोई शांत देवता भी योद्धा जैसे [[centre-of-mass|संतुलन]] के साथ चलता है।

इसका नाम एक पहेली है। कुछ कहते हैं कि यह छाया या मुखौटे के लिए किसी संस्कृत शब्द से आया है। दूसरे इसे "छावनी" से जोड़ते हैं, यानी सेना का पड़ाव। विद्वान अब भी एकमत नहीं हैं।

पुरुलिया छऊ सबसे भड़कीला है। नर्तक बाहर निकली आँखों वाले विशाल मुखौटे पहनते हैं, जो चटक रंगों से रँगे और मोतियों, चमकीली पन्नी और मोरपंखों से सजे होते हैं। सिर का साज नर्तक के अपने सिर से भी ऊँचा हो सकता है। मुखौटे का भाव नहीं बदल सकता, इसलिए नर्तक पूरे शरीर से अभिनय करते हैं, बड़ी-बड़ी छलाँगों और कलाबाज़ियों के साथ।

झारखंड का सरायकेला छऊ सदियों तक स्थानीय राजपरिवार के सहारे पला। इसके मुखौटे छोटे, चिकने और ज़्यादा नाज़ुक होते हैं। हरकतें सधी हुई और सुंदर होती हैं। कुछ नाचों में पूरी लड़ाई की जगह एक ही किरदार होता है, जैसे मोर, हिरण या नाविक।

[[@odisha|ओडिशा]] का मयूरभंज छऊ बिल्कुल मुखौटे नहीं पहनता। नर्तक चेहरा शांत और स्थिर रखते हैं, और शरीर को कहानी कहने देते हैं।

पुरुलिया के बहुत-से मुखौटे पश्चिम बंगाल के चड़िदा गाँव से आते हैं, जहाँ परिवार पीढ़ियों से मुखौटे बनाते हैं। वे हर मुखौटा मिट्टी के साँचे पर गढ़ते हैं, उस पर गोंद में भीगे कागज़ और कपड़े की परतें चढ़ाते हैं। सूखने पर खोल को उतार लिया जाता है, फिर रँगा और सजाया जाता है।

राक्षस का एक बड़ा मुखौटा पूरा होने में कई दिन लग सकते हैं। रंगाई सबसे आखिर में होती है: देवताओं के लिए सफ़ेद या गुलाबी, राक्षसों के लिए तीखे लाल, हरे और काले, और भौंहें जो लपटों की तरह ऊपर उठती हैं। चड़िदा के कलाकार अब घरों और तोहफ़ों की दुकानों के लिए छोटे मुखौटे भी बनाते हैं। 2018 में पुरुलिया छऊ मुखौटे को भौगोलिक संकेत टैग मिला, जो इस इलाके के कारीगरों के लिए यह नाम सुरक्षित रखता है।

पुरुलिया की सबसे पसंदीदा कहानी है देवी दुर्गा का भैंसे वाले राक्षस महिषासुर को हराना। यही कथा हर शरद में पूरे बंगाल में मनाई जाने वाली [[@durga-puja|दुर्गा पूजा]] के दिल में है।

छऊ परंपरागत रूप से चैत्र पर्व के आसपास नाचा जाता है, जो मार्च-अप्रैल के आसपास का बसंत का त्योहार है। गाँवों में खुले मैदानों में, दीयों और फ़्लडलाइट की रोशनी में, प्रदर्शन देर रात तक चल सकते हैं।

text: An advert is a message paid for by someone who wants you to buy something, use a service or believe an idea. Its job is to persuade, not just to inform.

Adverts use a set of well-tested tricks. They repeat a brand name until it feels familiar. They link a product with happy feelings, music, cute animals or famous faces. They create urgency with "limited offer" or "only three left". They show "everyone" using something, so you feel left out if you don't. Knowing these tricks doesn't make adverts stop working, but it helps you think before you buy.

st.reveal: A claim like this might come from a tiny survey, or dentists may have been allowed to pick several brands. The UK's advertising regulator once ruled against a famous toothpaste advert for exactly this kind of claim. Good questions about numbers are the best defence.

myth: Adverts only work on people who aren't paying attention.

sec.h: A little girl in polka dots
sec.t:
Since 1966, the [[@amul|Amul]] girl has appeared on Indian billboards, making jokes about the week's news. She is a lesson in how a simple character, seen again and again, can make a brand feel like an old friend. Familiarity is one of advertising's strongest tools. People tend to trust names they have seen many times.

Most of us believe we see through all this. In 1983, the sociologist W. Phillips Davison described what he called the "third-person effect": people tend to think adverts and media messages sway others more than themselves. Studies since then have often found that people are influenced more than they admit.

Colours are chosen carefully too. Many fast-food chains use red and yellow, which are bold and easy to spot, and many banks use blue, a [[@colour-meaning|colour]] often linked with calm and trust.

sec.h: Ads that don't look like ads
sec.t:
Today, many adverts don't look like adverts. A video-maker might use a product in a video because a company paid them. A brand might pay to place its drink in a film. On [[@social-media|social media]], apps use what they know about you to choose which ads you see.

Rules try to keep this honest. In India, the Advertising Standards Council of India, a watchdog set up by the industry in 1985, says that since 2021, influencers must clearly label paid posts. The US Federal Trade Commission has similar rules. Ads aimed at children face extra limits in many countries, because younger children often can't tell an advert from a programme.

sec.h: Reading an advert like a detective
sec.t:
When an advert makes a claim, ask who paid for it and what they want. Look for the small print. Words like "up to 50% off" or "helps fight germs" can promise less than they seem.

Numbers can be slippery too. "Nine out of ten people prefer it" may come from a tiny or carefully chosen group. Learning how [[@statistics-lies|statistics can mislead]] is one of the best defences. Adverts also pay for much of what you enjoy for free, from television channels to video apps, which is why they are everywhere.

text: A border is an agreed line where one country's laws stop and another's begin. On one side, you use one [[currency|currency]], follow one set of rules and carry one passport. Step across, and all of that can change.

Borders are decided by people. Some follow natural features like mountains and rivers. Some are straight lines drawn on [[@maps-flat|maps]]. Many were settled by [[treaty|treaties]] after long talks, and some after wars.
Borders have changed many times in history. Maps from different countries sometimes show the same border differently, because the countries disagree.

frames.cap: Some borders follow natural lines, like mountain ridges or rivers.
Many are decided by agreements, called treaties, between countries.
In 1947, the border between India and Pakistan was drawn in about five weeks, by a lawyer who had never been to India before. Millions of lives changed.
Today, countries try to settle border questions by talking, through courts and treaties. Some are still being discussed.

quiz.prompt: Which two countries share the longest border in the world?
quiz.reveal: The border between the USA and Canada runs for about 8,900 km, across forests, prairies, lakes and mountains, including the stretch with Alaska. Much of it follows a straight line of latitude, the 49th parallel.

d.try: Lay a piece of string across a table to split it between you and a friend. Agree on rules for your border. Can things be passed across? What if something rolls over the line? Then move the string to give one side a bowl of snacks, and notice how quickly the arguing starts.
myth: Borders have always been where they are now.
Most borders on today's maps are less than 200 years old, and many are under 100. Countries have split, joined and redrawn their lines many times, and some borders are still disputed.

sec.t:
Natural borders are the oldest kind. The [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]] separate India from Tibet for long stretches, and rivers divide many countries. But rivers change course after floods, which can leave land on the "wrong" side.

Straight-line borders were usually drawn by distant governments. Much of the US–[[@canada|Canada]] border follows the 49th parallel, a line of [[latitude|latitude]], one of the map [[@coordinates|coordinates]] used to find places. In Africa, European [[empire|empires]] drew many straight borders in the late 1800s, often splitting communities who spoke the same language.

sec.h: A line drawn in five weeks
Islands of one country inside another
sec.t:
For centuries, the border between India and [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]] near Cooch Behar was a tangle. There were 162 [[enclave|enclaves]]: small pockets of Indian land inside Bangladesh, and Bangladeshi land inside India. One was even an Indian pocket inside a Bangladeshi pocket inside India.

People living in them often could not easily reach schools or hospitals in their own country. In 2015, the two governments agreed to swap the enclaves. Residents could choose which country to belong to. Thousands of people became citizens of a country for the first time.

sec.h: Borders on the sea and in the sky
sec.t:
Borders don't stop at the coast. Under a UN agreement called the Law of the Sea, a country controls the waters up to about 22 km (12 nautical miles) from its shore, almost as if they were land. Further out, up to about 370 km, it has special rights to fish and to drill for oil and gas.

This is why tiny islands can matter so much. Owning one can mean owning a huge area of sea around it. India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands and [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]] give it a large share of the Indian Ocean.

Countries also control the air above them. Planes need permission to fly over another country, and [[@jobs-pilot|pilots]] radio ahead as they cross from one country's airspace into the next.

In the Belgian town of Baarle-Hertog, the border with the Netherlands runs through shops and homes. Some front doors are in one country and the back rooms in the other.

At Attari–Wagah, between Amritsar in India and Lahore in Pakistan, soldiers from both sides perform a flag-lowering ceremony every evening, with high kicks and loud cheers from crowds.

Today, most countries try to settle border questions by talking, through treaties or international courts. Some borders, including parts of India's, are still being discussed. Crossing most borders legally means showing a [[@passports|passport]], a reminder that these invisible lines still matter to everyone who travels.

text: An equation is a statement that two things are equal. It has an equals sign in the middle, with something on the left and something on the right. 4 + 3 = 7 is an equation. So is x + 3 = 7, where x stands for a number we need to find.

You can think of an equation as a balance scale that is perfectly level. Whatever is on the left weighs exactly the same as what is on the right. To solve it, you change both sides in the same way, so the scale stays level, until the unknown is alone on one side. Take 3 from both sides of x + 3 = 7 and you get x = 4.

st.prompt: A balance scale has a bag of marbles plus 3 loose marbles on one side and 11 loose marbles on the other. It is level. How many marbles are in the bag?
st.reveal: Take 3 marbles off each side and the scale stays level. Now the bag balances 8 marbles. As an equation: b + 3 = 11, so b = 8.

myth: An equation always has exactly one answer.
Some equations have two answers, some have many, and some have none. x × x = 9 is true for both 3 and −3. x + 1 = x has no answer at all, because adding 1 always changes a number.

sec.h: The birth of the equals sign
sec.t:
For most of history, people wrote "is equal to" in words, in whatever language they used. Then, in 1557, a Welsh doctor and mathematician named Robert Recorde wrote a maths textbook in English called *The Whetstone of Witte*.

In it, he introduced a sign made of two short parallel lines. He explained that he chose them because no two things could be more equal than a pair of parallel lines. His lines were much longer than ours, but the idea caught on. The plus and minus signs had first appeared in print only about 70 years earlier, so maths was slowly learning to write in symbols.

Equations themselves are far older than the equals sign. About 3,800 years ago, scribes in Babylon, in [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], pressed maths problems into clay tablets. Some asked questions like: a field's length and width together make a certain number, and its area is another number. What are the sides? Today we would call that a quadratic equation, one with a squared unknown.

In India, mathematicians such as [[@brahmagupta|Brahmagupta]], in the 7th century, wrote general rules for solving equations, including quadratic ones. Later, Sridhara gave a method that works much like the formula students learn in school today.

sec.h: Doing the same to both sides
sec.t:
The golden rule of equations is fairness. Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other. Add, subtract, multiply or divide, as long as you do it to both sides, and the equation stays true.

Suppose 3 notebooks and a ₹20 pen cost ₹110. Write it as 3n + 20 = 110. Take 20 from both sides: 3n = 90. Divide both sides by 3: n = 30. Each notebook costs ₹30. In dollars or rupees, the steps are the same.

You can always check your answer by putting it back in. Three notebooks at ₹30 make ₹90, and the pen adds ₹20, giving ₹110. The two sides match, so the answer is right. Mathematicians call this substituting, and it catches a lot of careless mistakes.

{{story:weather-forecasts}}

Scientists use equations as short descriptions of how the world works. Isaac [[@newton-life|Newton]] wrote that force equals mass times [[acceleration|acceleration]]: push harder and an object speeds up faster. Albert [[@einstein|Einstein]]'s E = mc², from 1905, says that a tiny amount of mass holds an enormous amount of energy.

Some equations are too hard to solve with pencil and paper. To forecast tomorrow's rain, computers solve huge numbers of equations about air pressure, temperature and wind, for millions of points across the Earth. That is why [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]] need some of the fastest computers in the world. And every one of those calculations still follows Recorde's two little lines.

text: Per cent means "out of a hundred". The words come from Latin, per centum, meaning "for each hundred". So 25 per cent, written 25%, means 25 out of every 100, which is the same as a quarter.

Percentages make it easy to compare things of different sizes. Scoring 45 out of 50 in one test and 72 out of 80 in another is hard to compare at a glance. Turn both into percentages and you get 90% each. That is why percentages appear on exam results, phone [[@batteries|batteries]], [[@discounts|sale signs]], [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]] and food packets.

st.prompt: A shop takes 50 per cent off a toy, then takes another 50 per cent off the new price. What do you pay?

options.t: A quarter of the original price

st.reveal: The first 50 per cent off halves the price. The second 50 per cent is taken from that smaller price, so it halves it again. Half of a half is a quarter, so you pay 25 per cent of what it first cost.

d.try: Ask 20 people a simple question, like "Do you prefer mangoes or bananas?" Count the answers. Since 20 times 5 is 100, multiply each count by 5 to get a percentage. If 13 people chose mangoes, that is 65 per cent. Draw your results as a bar chart.
myth: If something goes up by 50 per cent and then down by 50 per cent, it is back where it started.

The second change is worked out from a bigger number. If 100 rupees rises by 50 per cent, it becomes 150. A 50 per cent fall from 150 takes off 75, leaving 75 rupees, which is less than you began with.

Emperor Augustus taxed some sales at 1 per cent

sec.t:
A percentage is really a fraction with 100 on the bottom. 50% is 50/100, which is a half. 10% is 10/100, or a tenth. 1% is one hundredth.

To find a percentage of something, change it to a [[@fractions|fraction]] or a [[@decimals|decimal]] and multiply. Ten per cent is easiest: just divide by ten. So 10% of 350 rupees is 35 rupees. Twenty per cent is double that, and 5% is half of it. With these tricks, you can work out most discounts in your head.

Your phone battery shows a percentage so you can tell at a glance how much charge is left. A weather forecast that says a 70% [[@chance-weather|chance of rain]] means that on days with conditions like these, it rained about 7 times out of 10.

Percentages describe our planet and our bodies too. About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by [[@ocean-zones|ocean]]. Roughly 60% of an adult's body weight is water, which is one reason you need to [[@water-drink|drink water]] every day. In India, board exam results are given as percentages. Many American schools turn percentages into letter grades, so 90% and above often earns an A.

Percentages can fool people. Suppose a shirt costs 1,000 rupees. The price rises by 10%, to 1,100. Then it falls by 10%. Ten per cent of 1,100 is 110, so the new price is 990 rupees. The rise and fall were the same percentage, but they were taken from different amounts.

Advertisers know that big percentages sound impressive. "Now with 50% more!" might mean a [[@chocolate-making|chocolate]] bar went from 20 grams to 30 grams. Newspapers sometimes report that a risk has "doubled", a 100% increase, when it went from 1 in a million to 2 in a million. Both are true, but the second way sounds much scarier.

Can you have more than 100%? Yes, when you compare with a starting amount. If a tree grows from 2 metres to 5 metres, its height has increased by 150%. But you cannot score 110% in a test marked out of 100, and nobody can really give "110 per cent effort". There is only so much of you to give.

text: A ratio compares two or more amounts. If a [[@maths-recipes-scale|recipe]] uses 2 cups of water for every 1 cup of rice, the ratio of water to rice is 2:1. The real amounts can change, but the ratio stays the same. Two cups of rice need four of water. Half a cup needs one.

That is why ratios are so useful in the kitchen. They let you cook for one person or for twenty, without a new recipe each time. Many experienced cooks don't follow written recipes at all. They carry a handful of ratios in their heads and adjust by look, smell and [[@tongue-taste|taste]].

st.prompt: A lemonade recipe uses 1 cup of lemon juice to 4 cups of water. You want to make it with 3 cups of lemon juice. How much water do you need?
st.reveal: The ratio 1:4 means four times as much water as juice. Three cups of juice need 3 × 4 = 12 cups of water. Adding 3 cups to both (making 7) would give a much sourer drink, because it changes the ratio.

myth: To make a recipe twice as big, you just double everything, including the cooking time.

Doubling the ingredients keeps the ratios right, but cooking time does not simply double. A bigger cake may need a lower heat and only a bit longer, and a big pot of rice may need slightly less than double the water, because less steam escapes for each cup.

sec.t:
Cooking plain rice is a lesson in ratios. A common starting point is 1 part rice to 2 parts water, but it depends on the rice. Basmati often needs a little less water, and many cooks soak it first. Sticky short-grain rice needs a different amount, and a [[@pressure-cooker|pressure cooker]] needs less again, because less water escapes as steam.

In South India, idli and [[@dosa-idli|dosa]] batter starts with a ratio. Families often grind about 1 part urad dal to 3 or 4 parts rice, then leave the batter to ferment overnight. More dal gives softer, fluffier idlis. More rice gives crisper dosas. Each family argues that its own ratio is the right one.

Bakers are especially strict about ratios, because small changes can ruin a cake or loaf. The old pound cake used a pound each of flour, butter, sugar and eggs. Change one and the cake comes out dry, greasy or flat.

Many bread bakers use "baker's [[percentage|percentages]]". Flour is always 100%, and everything else is measured against it. A simple dough might be 100% flour, 65% water, 2% salt and 1% [[yeast|yeast]]. So 500 g of flour needs 325 g of water. This way, a baker in Mumbai and a baker in Chicago can share a recipe in any size.

Weighing ingredients is more reliable than using cups. A cup of flour can weigh quite different amounts depending on how tightly it is packed.

{{story:cooking-science}}

Suppose your recipe for 4 people uses 200 g of [[@cheese-paneer|paneer]] and you need to feed 6. The ratio of new people to old people is 6:4, or 1.5. So you multiply each ingredient by 1.5 and use 300 g of paneer.

But some things don't scale perfectly. Spices and salt are often added more carefully when cooking in large amounts, then adjusted to taste. Cooking time and heat also change. A big pot takes longer to heat through, and a large cake may need a cooler oven so the outside doesn't burn before the middle is cooked. This is where [[@cooking-science|cooking science]] comes in.

Even a cup of chai is a ratio problem. One home might use equal parts milk and water, another mostly milk. Then there is the ratio of tea leaves to liquid, and of sugar to everything. Change one and the [[@tea|tea]] tastes different.

Ratios also explain why lemonade can be too sour or too sweet. A recipe of 1 part lemon juice, 1 part sugar syrup and 4 parts water stays balanced however much you make. Add an extra cup of water without adding juice and you have changed the ratio, and the taste. Drinks factories work the same way, only with tanks instead of jugs.

text: Some numbers can be drawn as neat shapes made of dots. Triangular numbers are the totals you can arrange in a triangle: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 and so on. You get each one by adding the next counting number: 1, then 1 + 2, then 1 + 2 + 3.

Square numbers are the totals you can arrange in a square grid: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Each is a number multiplied by itself, so 5 × 5 = 25. Ancient Greek thinkers called these "figurate numbers", numbers with a figure or shape.

st.prompt: How many handshakes happen if 5 friends each shake hands once with everyone else?
st.reveal: The first friend shakes 4 hands, the next 3 new ones, then 2, then 1. That is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, a triangular number. Handshake puzzles always give triangular answers.

d.try: Use coins, buttons or bottle caps. Build triangles with rows of 1, then 1 and 2, then 1, 2 and 3, and count the totals. Now push two triangles next to each other, one the size of the other plus a row, and see if they make a square.
myth: Squaring a number always makes it bigger.
Only for numbers bigger than 1. Squaring 1 gives 1, and squaring a fraction makes it smaller, because half of a half is a quarter (0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25).
facts: Formula for the nth triangular number
Two triangular numbers next to each other always add up to a square

sec.t:
Look at a set of bowling pins: 1 in front, then 2, then 3, then 4. That's 10, the fourth triangular number. Snooker players start with 15 red balls packed in a triangle of five rows.

Fruit sellers often stack oranges or [[@apples|apples]] in pyramids on a cart. Each layer of a triangle-based pyramid is a triangular number, so the whole pile is a sum of triangular numbers. The Indian mathematician [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]], writing in 499 CE, gave rules for adding up series like these, including sums of squares and cubes.

Here is a neat link. Add any two triangular numbers that sit side by side in the list, and you always get a square. 1 + 3 = 4. 3 + 6 = 9. 6 + 10 = 16.

You can see why with dots. Draw a staircase-shaped triangle of 6 dots, then a slightly bigger one of 10 dots, flip it and fit it against the first. Together they fill a 4 × 4 square.

Squares hide another surprise. Add up odd numbers in order: 1, then 1 + 3, then 1 + 3 + 5. You get 1, 4, 9, 16. Each new odd number is an L-shaped strip wrapped around the previous square. This is one of many [[@number-patterns|number patterns]] you can see with your eyes rather than work out on paper.

On 10 July 1796, Gauss, then 19, wrote in his notebook: "Eureka! num = Δ + Δ + Δ". He had proved that every whole number can be written as the sum of at most three triangular numbers. For example, 20 = 10 + 10, and 25 = 15 + 10.

The ancient followers of [[@pythagoras|Pythagoras]] also treasured shape numbers. They gave special meaning to the tetractys, a triangle of ten dots in rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Square numbers sit underneath much of maths. The area of a square floor 4 metres on each side is 16 square metres. The Pythagorean theorem is a statement about squares on the sides of a triangle. Undoing a square, so going from 49 back to 7, is called taking a [[@square-roots|square root]], and it is one of the first steps into [[@algebra|algebra]].

text: A world record is the best result ever measured for something, checked by people who follow strict rules. Who checks depends on the kind of record. Sports records, like the fastest 100 m, are approved by the sport's own body, such as World Athletics. Records for almost everything else, from the longest [[@nails|fingernails]] to the biggest dosa, are judged by organisations such as Guinness World Records.
The key is fairness. A record must be measured the same way each time, with evidence that others can check. Otherwise nobody can say for sure that one result beats another.

st.prompt: A sprinter runs 100 m faster than the world record, but with a strong wind at her back. Does it count?

options.t: Only if the tailwind was 2 metres a second or less
Yes, the stopwatch is all that matters

sec.h: An argument at a shooting party
sec.t:
In 1951, Sir Hugh Beaver, the head of the Guinness brewery in Ireland, argued with friends about which game bird in Europe flew fastest. No book could settle it. He guessed that people in pubs had arguments like this every night.

So he hired twin brothers, Norris and Ross McWhirter, who ran a fact-finding agency in London. Their first book of records came out in 1955. By Christmas it was a bestseller in Britain. It has been published every year since, in dozens of languages.

India got its own record book in 1990, when the Limca Book of Records was first published. It lists feats by Indians and feats done in India, checked by its own editors.

In athletics, a record needs approved timing equipment, a measured track and a drug test. For sprints and long jump, a wind gauge also checks the breeze. A tailwind of more than 2 metres a second is enough to help, so the result cannot become a record.

[[@usain-bolt|Usain Bolt]]'s 100 m time of 9.58 seconds, set in Berlin in 2009, is still the men's record. That works out to an average [[@speed-distance|speed]] of about 37.6 km/h, roughly as fast as a car in a slow city lane. At his top speed he was going faster, about 44 km/h.

Records do not stand forever. Better training, food, shoes and tracks help athletes improve. Long-distance runners, for example, now run the [[@running-marathon|marathon]] in shoes with springy foam and stiff plates that save energy with every step. More people around the world now take part, so the chance of a rare talent turning up grows.

Sometimes records also fall because the rules change. [[@swimming|Swimming]] banned certain full-body suits after 2009, when dozens of records were broken in a short time. Officials decided the suits were doing too much of the work.

Some records may never be beaten. Robert Wadlow of Illinois, USA, who died in 1940, measured [[@body-height-limit|2.72 metres tall]]. That is about 70 cm taller than a standard doorway. His height came from a medical condition, and [[@growing-taller|how tall people grow]] usually depends on [[gene|genes]], food and health together.

sec.t:
कुछ नसें संदेश अंदर लाती हैं। त्वचा, आँखों, कानों, नाक और जीभ के [[sensor|सेंसर]] छूने, रोशनी, आवाज़, गंध और स्वाद की ख़बरें दिमाग की तरफ़ भेजते हैं। दूसरी नसें संदेश बाहर ले जाती हैं, [[@muscles|माँसपेशियों]] को हिलने और [[gland|ग्रंथियों]] को कुछ पदार्थ छोड़ने का हुक्म देती हैं।

ज़्यादातर समय दिमाग तय करता है कि क्या करना है। पर कुछ फ़ौरी काम मेरुरज्जु में ही निपटा दिए जाते हैं, जिन्हें [[@reflexes|रिफ़्लेक्स]] कहते हैं। कोई गर्म चीज़ छुओ, और दिमाग को गर्मी का पता चलने से पहले ही मेरुरज्जु बाँह को झटके से पीछे खींचने को कह देती है।

sec.h: स्क्विड, रफ़्तार और एक नोबेल पुरस्कार
sec.t:
स्क्विड के न्यूरॉनों में कुछ असामान्य रूप से मोटे नस-रेशे होते हैं, लगभग एक मिलीमीटर तक चौड़े। इसलिए 1930 और 1940 के दशक के औज़ारों से भी इन्हें परखना आसान था। इन्हीं की मदद से ब्रिटिश वैज्ञानिक एलन हॉजकिन और एंड्रयू हक्सले ने ठीक-ठीक समझा कि नस-संकेत कैसे चलता है। इसके लिए उन्हें 1963 के नोबेल पुरस्कार में हिस्सा मिला।

उससे पहले, 1850 में जर्मन वैज्ञानिक हरमन फ़ॉन हेल्महोल्ट्ज़ ने मेंढक की टाँग में नस की रफ़्तार नाप ली थी। यह बहुत लोगों की उम्मीद से कहीं धीमी निकली, बस लगभग 30 मीटर प्रति सेकंड।

सारी नसें बराबर तेज़ नहीं होतीं। बहुत-से रेशे माइलिन नाम की चिकनाई वाली परत में लिपटे होते हैं, जो कुछ-कुछ तार पर चढ़े प्लास्टिक के [[insulator|कुचालक]] खोल की तरह काम करती है। संकेत इस पर एक फ़ासले से दूसरे फ़ासले तक कूदते हुए लगभग 120 मीटर प्रति सेकंड तक पहुँच जाते हैं।

बिना माइलिन वाले पतले रेशे कहीं धीमे होते हैं, कभी-कभी 2 मीटर प्रति सेकंड से भी कम। अँगूठा टकराने का राज़ यही है। एक तेज़ नस [[@pain|दर्द]] की पहली तीखी चुभन लगभग फ़ौरन पहुँचा देती है। एक धीमी नस हल्का-हल्का दर्द एक पल बाद लाती है।

कुछ न्यूरॉन बहुत लंबे होते हैं। एक अकेली कोशिका रीढ़ के निचले सिरे से पैर के अँगूठे तक फैल सकती है, किसी लंबे इंसान में लगभग एक मीटर। साइटिक नस, जिसमें ऐसे बहुत-से रेशे होते हैं, शरीर की सबसे लंबी और सबसे चौड़ी नस है, ऊपर की ओर लगभग तुम्हारे अँगूठे जितनी मोटी।

दिमाग और मेरुरज्जु की नसें बुरी तरह चोट लगने पर ठीक से दोबारा नहीं उगतीं। इसीलिए [[@helmets|हेलमेट]] और सीटबेल्ट इतने ज़रूरी हैं। बाँहों और टाँगों की नसें कभी-कभी धीरे-धीरे भर जाती हैं, लगभग एक मिलीमीटर रोज़ की रफ़्तार से।

text: Every app or program starts as source code: instructions written by people in a programming language. Most companies keep their source code secret. Open-source software is different. Its code is published for anyone to read, use, change and share, usually for free.

That means a student in [[@kochi|Kochi]], a company in California and a volunteer in Brazil can all improve the same program. Some of the most important software on Earth is open source, including Linux, which runs most web servers, and the core of Android, which runs on billions of phones.

sec.t:
Think of source code as a recipe. With ordinary software, you can eat the cake but never see the recipe. With open source, the recipe is printed for everyone. You can bake it, add cardamom, share your version with friends, or point out that step five burns the bottom.

The rules for sharing are set out in a licence. Some licences say that if you share a changed version, you must also share your changes openly. Others let you use the code almost any way you like.

sec.h: A free system and a hobby project

sec.t:
Today Linux runs most of the computers behind websites, much of the [[@cloud-computing|cloud]], and every one of the world's 500 fastest [[@supercomputers|supercomputers]]. Android, the most common phone system, is built on Linux. The Firefox browser, the [[@python-scratch|Python programming language]] and the software behind [[@wikipedia-how|Wikipedia]] are open source too.

Governments use it as well. In 2015 the Government of India published a policy asking its departments to prefer open-source software where possible, partly to save money and avoid being locked in to one company.

It can seem odd that people write software and give it away. Some do it to learn, or for fun, or because they believe knowledge should be shared, the way public [[@libraries|libraries]] share books. Many companies pay their staff to work on open source because they rely on it and it's cheaper to improve shared code than to build everything alone. Others earn money by selling support, hosting or extra features.

Working openly also looks good. Many programmers get hired after employers see the code they have shared publicly.

Openness has a weak spot. Huge companies sometimes depend on small projects run by a few unpaid volunteers. In 2014 a bug called Heartbleed was found in OpenSSL, software that helps secure websites. It had gone unnoticed for about two years. In 2021 another flaw, in a free tool called Log4j, put millions of systems at risk.

Both were found and fixed because the code was open for anyone to inspect. Since then, companies and governments have started paying to support the volunteers who keep [[@internet-how|the internet]]'s hidden foundations standing.

text: Robots work all over space. Robotic arms catch spacecraft and move equipment on the International Space Station. Wheeled [[rover|rovers]] explore Mars and the Moon. Small flying robots float around inside the station, helping astronauts. And probes like the Voyagers, which are robots too, have travelled beyond the planets.
Robots go where it is too far, too dangerous or too expensive to send people. They do not need air, food or a ride home. Some keep working for years after their planned missions end.

sec.t:
One of the hardest workers in space is Canadarm2, a robotic arm about 17 metres long, longer than a school bus. Built by Canada, it has been on the space station since 2001. It helped assemble the station, catches cargo spacecraft and moves astronauts around on spacewalks.

It can "walk" across the outside of the station, end over end like an inchworm, by plugging into special sockets. A smaller two-armed robot, Dextre, rides on it to do fiddly jobs like changing batteries, so astronauts don't have to risk a spacewalk.

Perseverance carried a stowaway: Ingenuity, a helicopter weighing about 1.8 kg, lighter than a big bottle of water. Mars's air is about 100 times thinner than Earth's, so its blades had to spin very fast, around 2,500 times a minute. In April 2021, it made the first powered flight on another planet.

It was meant to make 5 test flights. It made 72, scouting routes for the rover. In January 2024, a damaged blade ended its flying days. It stayed switched on afterwards, sending back data from the spot where it last landed.

In August 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole. Its rover, Pragyan, rolled out down a ramp and travelled about 100 metres, studying the soil with lasers and X-rays. It confirmed sulphur in the Moon's surface near the pole. It even printed the Indian national emblem and ISRO's logo into the lunar dust with its wheels.

For the Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme, ISRO has built Vyommitra, a humanoid robot with a head, arms and a face. She is planned to fly on uncrewed test missions to check conditions before astronauts go.

Inside the space station, three cube-shaped robots called Astrobee have floated around since 2019. Named Honey, Queen and Bumble, they move using small fans, take pictures and test new tools. Earlier, a humanoid called Robonaut 2 worked on the station from 2011 to 2018. Japan sent a tiny talking robot, Kirobo, in 2013 to keep an astronaut company.

Robots have also gone farther than anything else humans have built. The [[@voyager|Voyager]] probes, launched in 1977, are still sending data from beyond the planets. The story of everything the rovers have found, from ancient riverbeds to strange rocks, is told in [[@mars-rovers|Mars rovers]]. And India's next step is putting people, not just robots, into [[orbit|orbit]] through [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]].

text: Aeroplanes first flew in India in December 1910, only seven years after the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]] first flew in the USA. European pilots shipped flimsy wood-and-cloth planes to India and flew them at shows in Calcutta and Allahabad, while crowds stared up in amazement.

The most famous early flight came on 18 February 1911. A 23-year-old French pilot, Henri Pequet, flew from Allahabad across the river Yamuna to Naini, about 10 km away, carrying around 6,500 letters. It is widely recognised as the world's first official airmail.

sec.t:
In November 1910, two Belgian pilots, Baron Pierre de Caters and Jules Tyck, arrived in Calcutta with their aircraft packed in crates. They flew several times from the grounds of the Tollygunge Club. On one flight in December, de Caters took up Mrinalini Sen, a Bengali writer, who became the first Indian woman to fly, as a passenger.

At about the same time, a British company, Humber, brought planes to an exhibition in Allahabad. Their pilots made flights there too, and they planned something new.

Planes then were very simple. They were made of wooden frames covered in cloth, held together with wires, and powered by engines weaker than a modern motorbike's. Pilots sat out in the open with no seatbelt. A gust of wind could flip them over, and many early pilots in Europe and America died in crashes. Flying in front of a crowd took real nerve.

{{story:airplanes-fly}}

The 1911 flight happened during the Kumbh Mela, when lakhs of pilgrims had gathered at Allahabad, now Prayagraj, where the Ganga and Yamuna meet. The organisers wanted to raise money for a students' hostel, so they asked people to send letters by air for a small extra fee.

Pequet took off in a Humber-Sommer biplane, a fragile machine with an open seat. The mailbags were strapped in beside him. He flew low over the river and landed at Naini about 13 minutes later. A postal official took the bags and sent the letters onward by ordinary post. Each envelope was stamped "First Aerial Post, U.P. Exhibition, Allahabad 1911".

The idea caught on fast. Later in 1911, Britain flew mail between London and Windsor to mark the crowning of King George V. In the USA, the first official airmail flight took place on Long Island in September 1911, and the US Post Office began regular airmail flights in 1918.

For the next 20 years, flying in India was mostly for adventurers, the army and rich hobbyists. That changed with a young man named JRD Tata. In 1929, he received the very first pilot's licence issued in India.

On 15 October 1932, he flew a small single-engine de Havilland Puss Moth from Karachi to Bombay, via Ahmedabad, carrying mail. It was the first flight of Tata Air Lines. In 1946, that company became Air India.

Indian women followed fast. In 1936, Sarla Thakral earned her flying licence in Lahore, and she wore a sari in the cockpit. She was not the very first Indian woman to get one, but she became the most famous, and her story is told in [[@hist-first-woman-pilot-india|India's first woman pilot]].

In 1911, a 10 km trip was headline news. Today, India's airlines fly more than 4 lakh passengers on busy days (2025) within the country alone, and non-stop flights connect Bengaluru to San Francisco in about 16–17 hours. And the [[@indian-air-force|Indian Air Force]], which now flies jets faster than sound, began in the very same year as JRD Tata's first mail flight, with just a handful of planes and pilots.

text: Dogs have been working beside humans for thousands of years, so plenty have shaped history. Laika was the first animal to [[orbit|orbit]] Earth, in 1957. Sled dogs Togo and Balto helped carry medicine to a sick town in Alaska in 1925. Hachiko, a loyal dog in Tokyo, became a symbol of devotion in Japan.

Other dogs saved lives with their noses or their courage. Barry the St Bernard rescued travellers lost in the Alps. In Mumbai, a police dog named Zanjeer helped find hidden weapons and explosives after the 1993 bomb blasts.

st.prompt: In 1925, why did the medicine for Nome, Alaska, go by dog sled instead of by plane or train?

options.t: Winter cold and the lack of roads or railway made dogs the safest way
The dogs were cheaper than fuel

st.reveal: The railway ended hundreds of kilometres away, there were no roads, and the few planes of the time struggled in deep winter cold and darkness. Experienced dog teams were the most reliable way to cross the frozen land.

d.try: Test your nose against a dog's. Ask an adult to hide a cotton ball dabbed with vanilla or orange peel somewhere in one room. Try to find it by smell alone. A trained dog's nose is thousands of times more sensitive, which is why police use them to search.
myth: Balto ran the whole serum run by himself and saved Nome.
It was a relay of about 20 drivers and around 150 dogs. Balto led the final team into Nome, so he became famous. Togo, led by musher Leonhard Seppala, ran the longest and most dangerous section.

sec.t:
In January 1925, a deadly disease called diphtheria broke out in Nome, a small town in Alaska. Children were most at risk. The only medicine, called serum, was hundreds of kilometres away. Winter had shut the sea, and the railway stopped far short of Nome.

So the serum went by dog sled, in a relay. About 20 drivers, called mushers, and roughly 150 dogs carried it about 1,085 km in about five and a half days, through blizzards and temperatures far below -40°C. A trip that normally took weeks was done in under six days.

The lead dog Togo and his musher Leonhard Seppala covered the longest and most dangerous leg, across sea ice that could crack. Balto led the last team into Nome. Newspapers made Balto a star, and a statue of him was put up in New York's Central Park that same year.

Hachiko was an Akita dog in [[@tokyo|Tokyo]]. Every evening he met his owner, a university professor, at Shibuya railway station. In 1925 the professor died suddenly at work and never came home.

Hachiko kept going to the station every day for about nine years, until he died in 1935. Commuters fed him and newspapers told his story. Today a bronze statue of him stands outside Shibuya station, one of Tokyo's most famous meeting points.

A dog's nose has hundreds of millions of scent [[receptor|receptors]], far more than ours, as explained in [[@power-dogs-nose|a dog's nose]]. That makes dogs superb searchers.

Barry, a St Bernard at a mountain [[monastery|monastery]] in the Swiss Alps in the early 1800s, is credited with saving about 40 people. Mountain teams still use dogs to find people buried in snow.

In March 1993, bombs went off across Mumbai. A Labrador police dog named Zanjeer helped search the city. He sniffed out grenades, rifles and explosives hidden in scooters and suitcases. When he died in 2000, Zanjeer was given a funeral with full police honours.

In the First World War, a stray dog named Stubby was smuggled to France by an American soldier. He learned to warn troops of gas attacks and incoming shells. He became one of the most famous dogs of the war and met three US presidents.

Dogs first lived with people when early humans tamed wolves, at least 15,000 years ago, though scientists still debate exactly when and where. That ancient friendship is told in [[@dogs-domestic|domestic dogs]].

text: Living next to a volcano sounds like a terrible idea. Yet hundreds of millions of people do it, and many have good reasons.

Volcanic ash and [[lava|lava]] break down into some of the most [[fertile|fertile]] soil on Earth, so farms near volcanoes can grow rich crops. Volcanoes bring hot water and heat that can warm homes and make electricity. They give useful stone and minerals, and they attract tourists. Many volcanoes erupt only rarely, perhaps once in hundreds of years, so families can live there for generations without seeing an eruption. And for many people, it is simply home, where their families have always lived.

st.prompt: Out of every ten people on Earth, about how many live within 100 km of an active volcano?

options.t: Fewer than one in a thousand

st.reveal: A 2015 study estimated around 800 million people live that close to a volcano that has erupted in the last 10,000 years or so. Most of them are in Indonesia, the Philippines, Japan, Central America and Italy.

d.try: With an adult's help, fill two pots, one with sandy soil and one with garden compost or soil mixed with a little ash from a cold, finished cooking fire. Plant a few mustard or methi seeds in each and water them the same. Watch which grows better over two weeks.
myth: Volcanoes erupt suddenly, without any warning.

Most eruptions are preceded by signs such as small earthquakes, swelling ground and changing gases. In 1991 scientists in the Philippines read these signs at Mount Pinatubo and helped evacuate tens of thousands of people before a huge eruption.

sec.t:
When volcanic rock and ash break down, they release [[nutrient|nutrients]] such as potassium and phosphorus that plants need. That is why the island of Java, in Indonesia, is crowded with rice fields climbing up the slopes of its volcanoes.

Around Mount Vesuvius in Italy, farmers grow tomatoes, grapes and lemons on the dark volcanic soil. The coffee of Central America and some of the tea of Java also grow on volcanic slopes. Even in India, the black cotton soil of the Deccan Plateau formed from the lava of ancient [[@deccan|Deccan]] eruptions.

In Kagoshima, in southern Japan, the volcano Sakurajima sits across a bay from the city and erupts small amounts of ash many times a year. Residents check ash forecasts, much as others check for rain.

The city gives families yellow bags to fill with ash swept from gardens and roofs, then collects them from special points. Schoolchildren wear helmets on some walks to school. People there have grown used to it, as you can read in [[@japan-culture|Japan]].

Volcanoes are also a power source. In [[@iceland|Iceland]], heat from underground warms about nine in ten homes. Kenya, [[@world-philippines|the Philippines]], Indonesia and New Zealand produce electricity from [[geothermal|geothermal]] power plants that use steam from deep underground.

Hot springs near volcanoes have drawn bathers for thousands of years. In Japan, soaking in [[@geysers-hot-springs|onsen]], natural hot spring baths, is a much-loved tradition.

Scientists watch active volcanoes closely. They use seismometers to feel tiny [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]], GPS to measure if the ground is swelling, and instruments to sniff gases coming out of cracks. A rising number of small earthquakes and puffing gas can be signs that [[magma|magma]] is moving up.

In 1991, Philippine and US scientists saw these signs at Mount Pinatubo. They warned authorities, and tens of thousands of people were moved away before one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century. Thousands of lives were saved. India's only active volcano, Barren Island in the Andaman Sea, has no people living on it, but scientists still keep an eye on its eruptions.

text: Pick almost any record for wildness and the Philippines turns up. It is a country of 7,641 islands in the western Pacific, strung out over about 1,850 km from north to south, roughly the distance from Delhi to Bengaluru. Only about 2,000 of those islands have people living on them.

It sits on the Pacific "Ring of Fire", so it has volcanoes, earthquakes and about 20 typhoons a year. It also has some of the richest seas on Earth and animals found nowhere else. Its 11.3 crore people (2024 [[census|census]]) are famous for loving basketball, karaoke and very long Christmas holidays.

st.prompt: The Philippines got its name from a person. Who?
st.reveal: In 1543 a Spanish explorer named the islands after Prince Philip, who later became King Philip II of Spain. Spain ruled the islands for over 300 years, and the name stuck.

n.certNote: The island count changes with how small an island can be and whether it shows at high tide. The 7,641 figure comes from a 2016 government mapping survey.

d.try: Get a world map and count how many separate islands you can spot in the Philippines. Then look up the real number, 7,641. Ask yourself what a mapmaker should do with a rock that only shows up at low tide.
myth: Everyone in the Philippines speaks Spanish because Spain ruled it for centuries.
Very few Filipinos speak Spanish today. The official languages are Filipino and English, and more than 170 local languages are spoken, though thousands of Spanish words live on inside them.

sec.h: A country that keeps finding islands
sec.t:
For decades the official count was 7,107 islands. Then, in 2016, a government mapping agency used new satellite images and found 534 more. Most are tiny, some no bigger than a cricket field.

The islands are the tops of underwater mountains, many of them [[@volcano|volcanoes]]. Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991 and threw so much ash and gas into the sky that the whole planet cooled by about half a degree Celsius for a year or so. Mayon, another volcano, has one of the most perfect cone shapes in the world, like a child's drawing of a mountain.

Living on so many islands has made Filipinos great boat builders. For centuries, people moved between islands in wooden boats with bamboo outriggers, the same trick used across the Pacific by the [[@polynesians|Polynesians]].

High in the mountains of northern Luzon, the Ifugao people carved [[@rice|rice]] fields into steep slopes. From above, the terraces look like giant green staircases climbing to the clouds. Water flows down from forests at the top, field by field, without a single pump.

How old are they? People long said 2,000 years. Some recent digs suggest many were built in the last 400 years or so. Either way, UNESCO lists them as a World Heritage Site.

Ferdinand Magellan's fleet arrived in 1521, and Magellan was killed in a battle on the island of Mactan, against the forces of a local chief called Lapulapu. Spain later took control and ruled for over 300 years. That is why most Filipinos are Christian, why towns hold huge fiestas for their saints, and why Christmas songs play in shops from September.

In 1898 the USA took over, and stayed until 1946. The Americans left behind English, a love of [[@basketball|basketball]], and thousands of army jeeps. Filipinos stretched those jeeps, painted them in wild colours and turned them into jeepneys, shared minibuses that still carry millions of people a day.

Food tells the same mixed-up story. Adobo, the unofficial national dish, is meat stewed in vinegar, soy sauce and garlic. Spanish settlers gave it its name, Chinese traders brought the soy sauce, and the vinegar trick for keeping meat fresh in the heat is older than both.

The country sits right in the path of Pacific typhoons, the same kind of storm Americans call a [[hurricane|hurricane]]. People build on stilts, tie roofs down and move inland when warnings come. And the strangest part? The same warm water that feeds these storms also feeds those record-breaking reefs, which is why scientists studying [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]] keep a close eye on the western Pacific.

text: Garuda is a mighty bird from Hindu, Buddhist and Jain stories. He's usually shown with a human body, an eagle's beak, wings and talons. In Hindu belief he is the king of birds and the vahana, or carrier, of the god Vishnu. Paintings show Vishnu and the goddess Lakshmi riding on his back.

Garuda is famous for his strength, speed and loyalty. He's also the great enemy of snakes. His story appears in the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] and the Puranas, and he's still honoured in temples across India and Southeast Asia.

st.prompt: In the story, why did Garuda steal the pot of amrit, the drink of immortality, from the gods?

options.t: To free his mother from being a servant to the snakes

st.reveal: Garuda's mother, Vinata, lost a bet and became a servant to her sister Kadru, the mother of snakes. The snakes promised to free her if Garuda brought them amrit. He fought his way past the gods to get it, then outwitted the snakes so they never drank it.

myth: Garuda and Jatayu, the bird in the Ramayana, are the same.
They are different. Jatayu is the vulture-king who fought Ravana to save Sita. In some tellings Jatayu is the son of Aruna, Garuda's brother, which makes Garuda his uncle.

sec.h: A bet, a mother and the drink of life
sec.t:
The story begins with two sisters, Vinata and Kadru, both wives of the sage Kashyapa. Kadru became the mother of a thousand snakes, the nagas. Vinata laid two eggs. In some tellings, impatient, she broke one open early, and out came Aruna, half formed, who became the charioteer of the Sun.

The sisters made a bet about the colour of a heavenly horse's tail. Kadru cheated, and Vinata lost. As punishment she had to serve Kadru and the snakes. When Garuda hatched, blazing so brightly that the gods were frightened, he wanted to free his mother. The snakes set a price: bring us amrit, the drink of immortality.

Garuda flew far beyond India. As traders and teachers travelled to Southeast Asia, his stories went too. Indonesia, the country with the most Muslims in the world, uses the Garuda Pancasila as its national emblem, and its national airline is Garuda Indonesia. The emblem stands for Indonesia's national ideals, not religion.

Thailand's royal emblem shows Garuda, called Khrut, and it appears on government papers. In Mongolia, the capital Ulaanbaatar uses a Garuda in its emblem. In [[@world-indonesia|Indonesia]]'s Bali, the giant Garuda Wisnu Kencana statue towers about 120 m high including its base, taller than the Statue of Liberty.

In India, the Brahminy [[@kites-birds|kite]], a reddish-brown bird with a white head, is often linked with Garuda, and some people bow when they see one. The Indian Air Force named its special forces the Garud Commando Force. The Garuda Purana, one of the eighteen major Puranas, is often read after a death in Hindu families.

Temples like the Vishnu temples of South India often have a Garuda shrine facing the main deity. The 'Garuda Seva' festival at temples such as Tirumala draws huge crowds. In Buddhist stories, garudas are a whole race of giant birds who live on mountains. Real birds of prey can't carry gods, but some come close to Garuda's powers: a soaring [[@eagles-hunt|eagle]] can spot a rabbit from more than a kilometre away.

text: For most of India's history, stories were heard, not read. Few people could read, and books had to be copied by hand on palm leaves or birch bark. So stories travelled by voice, song, dance and pictures.

Priests chanted hymns. Grandmothers told tales at bedtime. Wandering singers performed epics in village squares. [[@art-cheriyal|Painters unrolled scrolls]] and sang the scenes. Actors and dancers turned the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the Mahabharata into plays that could last all night. Many of these traditions are still alive today.

st.prompt: How did Vedic priests make sure not a single syllable of the hymns changed over thousands of years?

options.t: They memorised each hymn in several patterns, including backwards and in pairs
They copied them onto gold plates
They only chanted them once a year

st.reveal: Students learned each hymn straight through, then word by word, then in patterns that repeat and reverse words, such as ab, ba, ab. Any slip in one pattern would clash with the others. These techniques helped keep the texts astonishingly accurate.

d.try: Make a story scroll. Tape several sheets of paper into a long strip and draw scenes from a story you know, one after another. Roll it up, then unroll it scene by scene as you tell the story to your family, the way a Patua or bhopa would.
myth: Stories passed on by word of mouth always change and can't be trusted.
Some oral traditions change a lot, but others are extremely precise. Vedic chanting kept the hymns nearly word-perfect for about 3,000 years, using careful memory techniques.

sec.t:
The hymns of the Vedas were composed in the [[@vedic-age|Vedic age]], roughly 3,000 years ago or more. They were passed down by heart from teacher to student for many centuries before they were written down.

Students learned each hymn in several patterns. First straight through, then word by word, then in pairs that go forward and back. One famous pattern, the ghanapatha, weaves words back and forth like a braid. This system worked as a built-in error check. Scholars say it kept the texts almost unchanged. In 2008, UNESCO listed Vedic chanting as part of the world's intangible heritage, meaning living traditions rather than buildings.

In Rajasthan, the bhopas, a community of priest-singers, perform the story of Pabuji, a local hero, using a [[@art-phad|phad]]: a long painted cloth crowded with scenes. They set it up at night, often outdoors, and sing and dance the story while a partner holds up a lamp to light each scene. A performance can go on until dawn.

In Bengal, Patuas paint scrolls called patachitras and sing as they unroll them, one frame at a time. Rajasthan also has the kaavad, a small wooden shrine with painted doors that open one by one as the story unfolds.

More than 2,000 years ago, sculptors carved [[@jataka-tales|Jataka tales]], stories of [[@buddha|the Buddha]]'s past lives, onto the stone railings and gateways of [[stupa|stupas]] at Bharhut and Sanchi. Pilgrims who couldn't read could walk around them and follow the stories in pictures.

{{story:puppetry}}

In Chhattisgarh, singers perform the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] in a style called Pandavani. The most famous, Teejan Bai, holds a decorated tambura in one hand and uses it as a club, a bow or a chariot as she acts out battles. She was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 2019.

In Andhra Pradesh, Burra katha teams of three use drums and jokes to tell stories. In Tamil Nadu, Villu Paatu singers play a huge bow strung with bells. Harikatha performers in many states mix storytelling, music and teaching. A good performer reads the crowd, adding jokes for children and lingering on the scenes the audience loves best.

Every autumn, towns across north India stage the Ramlila, acting out the Ramayana over many nights before Dussehra. UNESCO recognised it in 2008. In Karnataka, [[@yakshagana|Yakshagana]] troupes perform epics through the night with tall headdresses and loud drums. In Kerala, [[@kathakali|Kathakali]] dancers tell stories with [[@art-kathakali-makeup|face paint]] and hand gestures.

[[@puppetry|Puppetry]] is another old storyteller. Rajasthani string puppets and shadow puppets from Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka have played epics for centuries.

Watching and listening together turned stories into shared events. A village might know every word of a scene and still cheer when the hero appears. That shared [[@memory|memory]] kept the stories alive long before printing came, and it still does.

text: Instant noodles are noodles that have been cooked and then fried or dried at a factory, so they need only a few minutes in hot water. They were invented in Japan in 1958. In India, Nestlé launched Maggi 2-minute noodles in 1983, and the yellow packet soon became a part of growing up for millions of children.

They caught on because they were cheap, quick, filling and easy enough for a hungry child or a tired hostel student to make. Clever [[@advertising|advertising]] helped. So did the masala tastemaker, which gave the noodles a flavour that felt familiar to Indian tongues. Today almost every hill-station stall and college canteen in India has a version on the menu.

st.prompt: Why do instant noodles cook so fast?

options.t: They were already steamed and fried at the factory
They are made from a special quick-cooking flour
They are much thinner than normal noodles

st.reveal: The noodles are cooked, then fried in hot oil or dried. Frying drives out the water and leaves tiny holes, so hot water rushes back in and softens them within minutes.

src: Momofuku Ando Instant Ramen Museum (CUPNOODLES Museum), Osaka, Japan.

d.try: Read the packet of any instant noodles at home. Find the salt (sodium) per serving and compare it with an adult's daily limit, which the WHO sets at under 2,000 mg of sodium. Then work out what share of a day's salt one packet holds.
myth: Instant noodles have a coating of wax that stays in your stomach for days.
There is no wax. The shine comes from the oil used to fry the noodles. Your body digests them like other foods made of flour and oil.

sec.t:
Maggi was a Swiss brand long before it made noodles. Julius Maggi began selling ready-made soups and seasonings in Switzerland in the 1880s, partly to give factory workers quick, cheap, nourishing meals. The company later became part of Nestlé.

When Maggi noodles arrived in India, the adverts promised a snack ready in two minutes, made by children for themselves after school. In practice, most people take a little longer. Families invented their own versions too: with peas and onions, with an egg, with extra chilli, or with cheese. On mountain treks in [[@himachal|Himachal]] and [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]], a steaming plate of Maggi at a roadside stall is almost a tradition.

In June 2015, India's food regulator, the [[@food-labels|FSSAI]], ordered Maggi noodles off shop shelves. It said tests had found lead above the allowed limit, and objected to a label that said "no added [[@food-science-umami|MSG]]". Nestlé disagreed, but withdrew and destroyed huge stocks of noodles already in shops.

In August 2015, the Bombay High Court overturned the ban, and fresh tests found the noodles within safe limits. Maggi returned to shops in November that year. The episode made many families read food packets more carefully.

Instant noodles are mostly refined flour, oil and salt. A single packet can hold close to half of the [[@salt|salt]] that health experts suggest for an adult in a whole day, and not much fibre, [[vitamin|vitamins]] or [[protein|protein]].

That does not make them poison. Nutritionists usually suggest treating them as an occasional snack rather than a daily meal, and adding vegetables, an egg or paneer to make a bowl more filling. The noodles took over India because they solved a real problem: getting hot food on the table quickly, for very little money.
